business.title: Diagnosis and causal-chain-based treatment of water-leakage in in-service mountainous highway tunnels: an engineering application
business.description: Water leakage in in-service mountainous highway tunnels is difficult to diagnose due to concealed geological conditions, coupled seepage processes, and frequent recurrence after local repair. This study proposes a causal-diagnosis and causal-chain-based treatment framework for tunnel water leakage. The water-leakage mechanism is interpreted as a progressive process involving groundwater recharge, fracture-controlled seepage transport, drainage obstruction, water-pressure accumulation behind the lining, and failure at weak points in the waterproofing system. A diagnostic method integrating leakage characteristics, groundwater conditions, geological anomalies behind the lining, drainage performance, and waterproofing defects is established, followed by a three-stage treatment strategy. The framework was applied to the Dashiling Tunnel on the Shenzhen–Cenxi Expressway (G2518), China, using leakage surveys, seismic reflection imaging, and visual inspections. A total of 312 leakage defects were identified, with 48.1% occurring at secondary-lining construction joints and 37.8% occurring in wall-foot-to-sidewall zones. Fracture-related anomalies behind the lining and severe blockage in 50.0% of the inspected side drains revealed a compound leakage mechanism. After targeted treatment, two years of monitoring showed that the total area of pavement leakage was reduced to approximately 3.9% of its pre-treatment level. The number of tunnel water-leakage defects exhibited an approximately linear decreasing trend, with an overall reduction of more than 70%. The densities of tunnel water-leakage defects in all statistical sections were less than 0.3 points per linear meter, demonstrating good treatment effectiveness. The proposed framework provides a practical approach for the systematic diagnosis and treatment of water leakage in comparable in-service mountainous highway tunnels with similar hydrogeological and drainage conditions.

science.title: Blockchain-assisted revocable capability credential authentication for cross-domain UAVs
science.description: Cross-domain UAV operations require secure and privacy-preserving authentication across multiple administrative domains. However, existing schemes still suffer from centralized authorization, exposure of mission attributes, insufficient revocation consistency, and limited auditability. To address these issues, this paper proposes a blockchain-assisted revocable capability credential authentication protocol for cross-domain UAV edge networks. The main innovation is to shift cross-domain UAV authentication from identity- or location-centric verification to revocation-aware lifecycle verification of mission capabilities. In the proposed framework, a Domain Authority committee jointly issues blinded capability credentials through distributed key generation and threshold BLS signatures. UAVs then prove mission-policy compliance using Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs without revealing sensitive capability attributes. Meanwhile, the blockchain maintains credential active states, revocation versions, and audit-root evidence for cross-domain consistency and accountability. A ticket-based AuthResume mechanism is further designed to reduce repeated authentication overhead while preventing outdated tickets from bypassing revocation. Formal security analysis, BAN logic, and Scyther verification show that the protocol supports credential unforgeability, revocation enforcement, auditability, mutual authentication, freshness, and session synchronization. Solidity smart contracts were deployed on the Sepolia testnet, and experimental results demonstrate acceptable FullAuth overhead and lightweight repeated access through AuthResume.

science.title: Enhancing ferric-reducing antioxidant activity through terpene mixture optimization
science.description: The present study investigated the antioxidant potential of three terpenes p-cymene, thymol, and β-ionone—through their ferric reducing power (FRAP). Individually, p-cymene demonstrated the strongest activity with an EC50 of 123.03 ± 2.05 µg/mL, followed by thymol (EC50 = 153.16 ± 2.84 µg/mL), whereas β-ionone exhibited the lowest ferric reducing capacity (EC50 = 931.46 ± 5.37 µg/mL), revealing significant variation in their antioxidant efficacy. To assess combinatorial effects, twelve randomized mixture trials were performed, each representing the mean of three independent repetitions, yielding FRAP EC50 values ranging from 79.76 to 931.46 µg/mL. Statistical analysis identified significant contributions from linear terms (β1, β2, β3), binary interactions (β12, β13), and the ternary interaction term (β123), indicating that both individual and combined effects shaped the overall antioxidant response. Analysis of 2D and 3D mixture plots suggested that an EC50 around 79.70 µg/mL could be obtained by combining all three terpenes. Furthermore, desirability analysis predicted an optimal FRAP EC50 of 58.23 µg/mL, achieved with a mixture comprising 17% β-ionone, 42% p-cymene, and 41% thymol, with a global desirability of 99.9%. These findings demonstrate that strategic blending of structurally related terpenes can substantially enhance ferric reducing capacity, providing a robust framework for the development of potent natural antioxidant formulations.
